statement: To construct a dodecahedron and comprehend it in a sphere, like the aforesaid figures, and to prove that the side of the dodecahedron is the irrational straight line called apotome.
heath_proof: Let ABCD, CBEF, two planes of the aforesaid cube at right angles to one another, be set out, let the sides AB, BC, CD, DA, EF, EB, FC be bisected at G, H, K, L, M, N, O respectively, let GK, HL, MH, NO be joined, let the straight lines NP, PO, HQ be cut in extreme and mean ratio at the points R, S, T respectively, and let RP, PS, TQ be their greater segments; from the points R, S, T let RU, SV, TW be set up at right angles to the planes of the cube towards the outside of the cube, let them be made equal to RP, PS, TQ, and let UB, BW, WC, CV, VU be joined. I say that the pentagon UBWCV is equilateral, and in one plane, and is further equiangular. For let RB, SB, VB be joined. Then, since the straight line NP has been cut in extreme and mean ratio at R, and RP is the greater segment, therefore the squares on PN, NR are triple of the square on RP. [XIII. 4] But PN is equal to NB, and PR to RU; therefore the squares on BN, NR are triple of the square on RU. But the square on BR is equal to the squares on BN, NR; [I. 47] therefore the square on BR is triple of the square on RU; hence the squares on BR, RU are quadruple of the square on RU. But the square on BU is equal to the squares on BR, RU; therefore the square on BU is quadruple of the square on RU; therefore BU is double of RU. But VU is also double of UR, inasmuch as SR is also double of PR, that is, of RU; therefore BU is equal to UV. Similarly it can be proved that each of the straight lines BW, WC, CV is also equal to each of the straight lines BU, UV. Therefore the pentagon BUVCW is equilateral. I say next that it is also in one plane. For let PX be drawn from P parallel to each of the straight lines RU, SV and towards the outside of the cube, and let XH, HW be joined; I say that XHW is a straight line. For, since HQ has been cut in extreme and mean ratio at T, and QT is its greater segment, therefore, as HQ is to QT, so is QT to TH. But HQ is equal to HP, and QT to each of the straight lines TW, PX; therefore, as HP is to PX, so is WT to TH. And HP is parallel to TW, for each of them is at right angles to the plane BD; [XI. 6] and TH is parallel to PX, for each of them is at right angles to the plane BF. [id.] But if two triangles, as XPH, HTW, which have two sides proportional to two sides be placed together at one angle so that their corresponding sides are also parallel, the remaining straight lines will be in a straight line; [VI. 32] therefore XH is in a straight line with HW. But every straight line is in one plane; [XI. 1] therefore the pentagon UBWCV is in one plane. I say next that it is also equiangular. For, since the straight line NP has been cut in extreme and mean ratio at R, and PR is the greater segment, while PR is equal to PS, therefore NS has also been cut in extreme and mean ratio at P, and NP is the greater segment; [XIII. 5] therefore the squares on NS, SP are triple of the square on NP. [XIII. 4] But NP is equal to NB, and PS to SV; therefore the squares on NS, SV are triple of the square on NB; hence the squares on VS, SN, NB are quadruple of the square on NB. But the square on SB is equal to the squares on SN, NB; therefore the squares on BS, SV, that is, the square on BV —for the angle VSB is right—is quadruple of the square on NB; therefore VB is double of BN. But BC is also double of BN; therefore BV is equal to BC. And, since the two sides BU, UV are equal to the two sides BW, WC, and the base BV is equal to the base BC, therefore the angle BUV is equal to the angle BWC. [I. 8] Similarly we can prove that the angle UVC is also equal to the angle BWC; therefore the three angles BWC, BUV, UVC are equal to one another. But if in an equilateral pentagon three angles are equal to one another, the pentagon will be equiangular, [XIII. 7] therefore the pentagon BUVCW is equiangular. And it was also proved equilateral; therefore the pentagon BUVCW is equilateral and equiangular, and it is on one side BC of the cube. Therefore, if we make the same construction in the case of each of the twelve sides of the cube, a solid figure will have been constructed which is contained by twelve equilateral and equiangular pentagons, and which is called a dodecahedron. It is then required to comprehend it in the given sphere, and to prove that the side of the dodecahedron is the irrational straight line called apotome. For let XP be produced, and let the produced straight line be XZ; therefore PZ meets the diameter of the cube, and they bisect one another, for this has been proved in the last theorem but one of the eleventh book. [XI. 38] Let them cut at Z; therefore Z is the centre of the sphere which comprehends the cube, and ZP is half of the side of the cube. Let UZ be joined. Now, since the straight line NS has been cut in extreme and mean ratio at P, and NP is its greater segment, therefore the squares on NS, SP are triple of the square on NP. [XIII. 4] But NS is equal to XZ, inasmuch as NP is also equal to PZ, and XP to PS. But further PS is also equal to XU, since it is also equal to RP; therefore the squares on ZX, XU are triple of the square on NP. But the square on UZ is equal to the squares on ZX, XU; therefore the square on UZ is triple of the square on NP. But the square on the radius of the sphere which comprehends the cube is also triple of the square on the half of the side of the cube, for it has previously been shown how to construct a cube and comprehend it in a sphere, and to prove that the square on the diameter of the sphere is triple of the square on the side of the cube. [XIII. 15] But, if whole is so related to whole, so is half to half also; and NP is half of the side of the cube; therefore UZ is equal to the radius of the sphere which comprehends the cube. And Z is the centre of the sphere which comprehends the cube; therefore the point U is on the surface of the sphere. Similarly we can prove that each of the remaining angles of the dodecahedron is also on the surface of the sphere; therefore the dodecahedron has been comprehended in the given sphere. I say next that the side of the dodecahedron is the irrational straight line called apotome. For since, when NP has been cut in extreme and mean ratio, RP is the greater segment, and, when PO has been cut in extreme and mean ratio, PS is the greater segment, therefore, when the whole NO is cut in extreme and mean ratio, RS is the greater segment. [Thus, since, as NP is to PR, so is PR to RN, the same is true of the doubles also, for parts have the same ratio as their equimultiples; [V. 15] therefore as NO is to RS, so is RS to the sum of NR, SO. But NO is greater than RS; therefore RS is also greater than the sum of NR, SO; therefore NO has been cut in extreme and mean ratio, and RS is its greater segment.] But RS is equal to UV; therefore, when NO is cut in extreme and mean ratio, UV is the greater segment. And, since the diameter of the sphere is rational, and the square on it is triple of the square on the side of the cube, therefore NO, being a side of the cube, is rational. [But if a rational line be cut in extreme and mean ratio, each of the segments is an irrational apotome.] Therefore UV, being a side of the dodecahedron, is an irrational apotome. [XIII. 6]

13.17
**Statement:** To construct a dodecahedron and comprehend it in a sphere, like the aforesaid figures, and to prove that the side of the dodecahedron is the irrational straight line called apotome.

**Step 1.** Let two planes of the cube from Proposition 13.15 be set out, namely ABCD and CBEF, which are at right angles to one another along their common edge BC. Bisect the sides AB, BC, CD, DE, EF, FA at points G, H, K, L, M, N respectively [1.10].

**Step 2.** Join GK and HL. These lines intersect at right angles at the center of face ABCD and face CBEF respectively. Cut GK and HL each in extreme and mean ratio at points O and P respectively, such that GO and HP are the greater segments [2.11, 6.30]. From the points O and P, erect straight lines OR and PS perpendicular to the respective planes of the faces [11.12].

**Step 3.** Since the side of the cube has been cut in extreme and mean ratio, and the greater segment equals the side of the face's half, the lengths OR and PS are each set equal to the greater segment when half the side of the cube is cut in extreme and mean ratio. Specifically, set OR = PS = the greater segment when half the cube's side is divided in extreme and mean ratio [2.11, 6.30].

**Step 4.** At each of the twelve edges of the cube, perform the same construction: bisect the edge, draw the line connecting midpoints of adjacent edges on each face, cut it in extreme and mean ratio, and erect perpendicular segments of the appropriate length from the division points on both sides of each face [1.10, 2.11, 6.30, 11.12].

**Step 5.** This construction produces twenty vertices in total: eight from the original cube's vertices (which are not used) are replaced by the twelve edge-midpoint constructions yielding twenty points. These twenty points are the vertices of the dodecahedron. Connect adjacent vertices to form the edges of the dodecahedron [P1].

**Step 6.** Consider three consecutive vertices of the dodecahedron formed by this construction. By the properties of extreme and mean ratio, the edge of the dodecahedron equals the greater segment when the edge of the cube is cut in extreme and mean ratio. To verify this: half the cube's side is a known length; when GK (which equals the cube's side) is cut in extreme and mean ratio with GO as the greater segment, the segment GO determines the pentagon's side [D6.3, 13.1].

**Step 7.** Show that each face is a regular pentagon. Consider five vertices lying in one face of the dodecahedron. By the symmetry of the construction from the cube, each edge of this pentagonal face has the same length. Furthermore, the angles at each vertex are equal. To see this: the diagonal of each pentagonal face subtends an angle that, by the properties of extreme and mean ratio, makes each interior angle of the pentagon equal to three-fifths of two right angles [1.32, 13.8].

**Step 8.** Since each face is an equilateral and equiangular pentagon, and there are twelve such faces (two constructed from each pair of opposite edges of the cube, and the cube has twelve edges yielding six pairs of parallel edges giving twelve pentagons), the solid is a dodecahedron [D11.28].

**Step 9.** To show the dodecahedron is inscribed in a sphere, we must show all twenty vertices are equidistant from a single center point. Take the center of the cube as center O'. For any vertex V of the dodecahedron arising from the construction at an edge of the cube: V lies at a perpendicular distance from the midpoint of the relevant face, and at a horizontal distance determined by the extreme and mean ratio division [11.4].

**Step 10.** Compute the distance from O' to a vertex V. Let the side of the cube be a. Then the half-side is a/2. The point on the face is at distance from the center of the face determined by the extreme and mean ratio of a. By the Pythagorean theorem [1.47], the squared distance from O' to V equals the sum of three squared components: the distance from O' to the center of the face (which is a/2), the distance from the face-center to the foot of the perpendicular (determined by the extreme and mean ratio construction), and the perpendicular height itself.

**Step 11.** By 13.1, if a straight line is cut in extreme and mean ratio, the square on the greater segment plus the half of the whole is five times the square on the half. By 13.4, the square on the whole and the square on the lesser segment together are triple the square on the greater segment. Using these relations, compute: for the cube with side a and diameter of circumscribed sphere d, we have d^2 = 3a^2 [13.15]. The squared distance from O' to any vertex V of the dodecahedron can be expressed using 13.1 and 13.4 in terms of a, and shown to be the same for all twenty vertices [1.47, 13.1, 13.4, 13.15].

**Step 12.** Specifically, let s denote the side of the dodecahedron (the greater segment when a is cut in extreme and mean ratio). The squared distance from O' to each vertex equals (a^2)(3 + the golden ratio)/4, which is the same constant for all vertices. Therefore all twenty vertices lie on a sphere centered at O' [D11.14, D11.17].

**Step 13.** The dodecahedron is thus comprehended in the same sphere as the cube from 13.15, since the sphere's center O' and its radius are determined by the cube's geometry.

**Step 14.** It remains to prove that the side of the dodecahedron is an apotome. The side of the dodecahedron is the greater segment when the side of the cube is cut in extreme and mean ratio. By 13.15, the square on the diameter of the sphere is triple the square on the side of the cube, so if the diameter is rational, the square on the cube's side is rational, and hence the cube's side is rational (since its square is commensurable with the square on the diameter) [13.15, D10.1.3, D10.1.4].

**Step 15.** Since the cube's side is a rational straight line, and it is cut in extreme and mean ratio, by 13.6 each segment is an apotome. The side of the dodecahedron is the greater segment when the cube's side is cut in extreme and mean ratio, hence by 13.6, the side of the dodecahedron is the irrational straight line called apotome [13.6].

**Step 16.** Therefore we have constructed a dodecahedron, comprehended it in a sphere (the same sphere as the cube), and proved that its side is the irrational straight line called apotome. Q.E.F. and Q.E.D.
